Lane snapper (Lutjanus synagris) is a moderately sized lutjanid commonly found over sandy and seagrass habitats throughout the western Atlantic. Field surveys of fully grown individuals indicate that females attain an ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range observed in this species across its distribution. Males also reach a maximum length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], suggesting an absence of marked sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size. The onset of reproductive capability in females is tied to a distinct size threshold, with puberty occurring at a total length of 23.8 centimeters [Lp = 23.8 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 183 grams [Wwp = approximately 183 grams] based on the species' length-weight relationship, a mass that females typically achieve during their second or third growing season. Such a size-based maturation schedule is common among tropical snappers and ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves before directing energy toward gamete production.

Reproductive output in Lutjanus synagris has been estimated through studies of closely related congeners and validated with field observations of spawning frequency. Under stable thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females are capable of producing an estimated approximately 3650 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3650 eggs per spawning event], with approximately 274 spawning events occurring each year [F_R_i = approximately 274 spawning events occurring each year]. This high-frequency reproductive strategy is characteristic of many tropical lutjanids and compensates for the relatively low fecundity per event by spreading reproductive effort across an extended spawning season. The daily egg production rate is consistent with the maximum output observed under favorable environmental conditions, reflecting an iteroparous life-history strategy that prioritizes repeated spawning over the production of a single large clutch. Such a pattern is well suited to the variable recruitment success typical of reef-associated fishes, where episodic environmental windows favor larval survival.

Early life stages of Lane snapper are characterized by extremely small neonatal size and rapid developmental events tied to water temperature. Newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs and undergo a brief yolk-sac phase before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of the closely related spotted rose snapper. This minute initial mass underscores the vulnerability of larvae during the first days post-hatch. The age at birth, encompassing the interval from fertilization to the completion of hatching and the assumption of free-swimming activity, is approximately 2.96 days [ab = approximately 2.96 days] when eggs are incubated at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This rapid developmental pace is typical of tropical lutjanids and allows larvae to begin exogenous feeding before their endogenous yolk reserves are fully exhausted, a critical adaptation for survival in oligotrophic waters.

Maximum longevity in Lutjanus synagris has been inferred from both tag-recapture studies and otolith-based age determinations. The oldest documented individuals reach a lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] when living under ambient thermal regimes averaging 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan is consistent with the slow-to-moderate growth rates and late maturity that define the life-history strategy of many large-bodied snappers. The species' ultimate wet weight, attained after somatic growth has effectively ceased, reaches approximately 2900 grams [Wwi = approximately 2900 grams]. This maximum body mass corresponds closely to the length-weight relationship derived for the species and is achieved by the oldest females and males in the population. The combination of moderate asymptotic size, delayed reproduction, and extended longevity places Lane snapper along a slow end of the fast-slow continuum among western Atlantic lutjanids, with important implications for its vulnerability to fishing pressure.

Comparative studies within the genus Lutjanus highlight several distinctive ecological features of Lane snapper. Unlike the more reef-obligate congener Lutjanus campechanus, L. synagris exhibits a broader habitat tolerance, frequently occurring over sand bottoms and seagrass meadows adjacent to reef structures. This habitat flexibility is reflected in its feeding ecology, which emphasizes crustaceans and small fishes rather than the piscivorous diet typical of larger snappers. The species' age at first reproduction aligns with its size-based maturation schedule, with females initiating spawning once they have surpassed the 23.8 centimeter [Lp = 23.8 centimeter] total length threshold corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 183 grams [Wwp = 183 grams]. Spawning aggregations are known to form seasonally in response to lunar cycles and water temperature, though the precise timing varies latitudinally. The protracted reproductive period and high annual fecundity, combined with a two-decade lifespan (approximately 20 years) [am = approximately 20 years], allow Lane snapper populations to buffer against intermittent recruitment failure, a demographic trait that has facilitated its persistence across a heavily exploited portion of its range at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
